contraindications: Not effective for individuals unable to identify or connect with personal values
May be less effective when emotional intensity is overwhelming and immediate regulation is required
original_extraction.evidence_text:
What do you cherish most in life? Health? Work? Family? Friends? Religion? Sport? Nature? It’s
no surprise that life is richer and more fulfilling when we actively invest our time and energy in the
things that are most important or meaningful to us. Yet all too often our attempts to avoid
unpleasant feelings get in the way of doing what we truly value.

---

For example, suppose you are a professional actor and you love your work. Then one day, quite out
of the blue, you develop an intense fear of failure just as you are due to appear onstage. So you
refuse to go on (a malady commonly known as ‘stage fright’). Refusing to go onstage may well
reduce your fear temporarily, but it also stops you from doing something you truly value.

---

Or suppose you’
ve just gone through a divorce. Sadness, fear and anger are all natural reactions, but
you don’t want to have these unpleasant feelings. So you try to lift your mood by eating junk food,
getting drunk or chain-smoking cigarettes. But what does this do to your health? I’ve never met
anyone who didn’t value their health, and yet many people use control strategies that actively
damage their physical bodies.

---

The degree of control we have over our thoughts and feelings depends largely on how intense they
are—the less intense the feelings, the more we can control them. For instance, if we’re just dealing
with the typical everyday stresses, a simple relaxation technique can make us feel calmer right
away. However, the more troubling our thoughts and feelings are, the less effective our attempts at
control will be. If you’re terrified, no relaxation technique known to humanity will calm you.
generation_rules: Use examples contrasting valued activities with avoidance due to unpleasant feelings
Illustrate the relationship between emotional intensity and control efficacy
Emphasize naturalness of unpleasant emotions and their interference with valued actions
pause_rules: Pause after questions to allow reflection on personal values
Pause after examples to emphasize the consequences of avoidance and control strategies
original_extraction.psychological_function: Highlighting the impact of emotional intensity on the ability to control thoughts and feelings; illustrating the limitations of control strategies in managing intense emotions; fostering awareness of maladaptive coping mechanisms that conflict with personal values.
repetition_rules: Reinforce the contrast between temporary relief from avoidance and long-term interference with values
Repeat the idea that intense emotions reduce control effectiveness
symbolic_elements: stage fright as fear of failure
divorce as a trigger for sadness, fear, and anger
junk food, alcohol, and cigarettes as mood-lifting but harmful control strategies
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Encouraging engagement with personally valued life domains despite unpleasant feelings; reducing avoidance behaviors that interfere with valued actions; promoting acceptance of natural emotional reactions rather than control or suppression.
voice_rules: Use direct questioning to engage reflection on personal values
Employ illustrative examples to demonstrate concepts
Maintain an explanatory and empathetic tone
